newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus opponents optimistic at 11th-hour talks.
newsitem.headline: Belarus opponents optimistic at 11th-hour talks.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, mediating in a tense standoff between political forces in Belarus, indicated on Friday he was optimistic a solution could be found.
Arriving with a smiling President Alexander Lukashenko at 11th-hour talks with Lukashenko's parliamentary rivals, Chernomrydin gave reporters a thumbs-up sign.
"We are in a good mood," he said.
Chernomrydin flew to Minsk on Thursday evening to try to defuse the standoff, which has developed over Lukashenko's plans to widen his powers by referendum.

With voting already under way and due to end on Sunday, Chernomyrdin's visit was a last-ditch attempt by Russia to head off a destabilising conflict in the small post-Soviet republic, its closest ally.
Chernomyrdin arrived in the Belarussian capital with leaders of the two Russian chambers of parliament -- a joint mission showing rare unity between Russia's executive and legislature.
While he spoke to Lukashenko, they met Belarus parliament speaker Semyon Sharetsky, who has been leading a bid to impeach the president if he goes ahead with the referendum.
The two sides then joined up for talks in the early hours of Friday morning, saying they had each hammered out compromise deals to put on the table.
"We have several compromise options which would lead to a "zero' (option)," said Gennady Seleznyov, speaker of Russia's lower house of parliament.
The Belarus parliament has indicated it might drop its impeachment plans -- Lukashenko's main demand -- if he compromises over the referendum.
Lukashenko told a rally earlier in Brest he would under no circumstances back down over the referendum.

But sources close to Lukashenko later told Reuters he had agreed to a compromise under which the referendum would still go ahead. Its results would be not be binding but would be taken into account in constitutional reforms which would follow,

Officials close to Sharetsky, who sat down with Lukashenko and the Russian mediators at a presidential meeting house in central Minsk, indicated that while not ideal, such a compromise might be acceptable.

As Chernomyrdin flew to Belarus, the U.S. State Department added its voice to a chorus of international concern at the growing political crisis, saying Lukashenko's attempt to expand his powers by referendum had created "instability and fear".

On Wednesday Lukashenko had spurned peace talks organised by Moscow in the Russian city of Smolensk, where Sharetsky met leaders of Russia's two parliamentary chambers and agreed the outline of a compromise deal.
On Thursday he told a rally of 10,000 people in the main square of Brest near the Polish border with Belarus that it would be "laughable" for him to scrap the referendum.
"I am not going to share power with anyone," he declared in an interview with Russia's Interfax news agency.
The Belarus constitutional court, whose rulings the president has repeatedly ignored, is due to meet later on Friday to discuss the impeachment bid, launched by 70 deputies.

Lukashenko would probably be able to stop the bid succeeding at the final stage, since his opponents would be unlikely to be able to muster the two-thirds majority of the 199 deputies required to remove him from power.
He, meanwhile, is seeking popular backing for major changes to the constitution which would extend his term by more than two years and tighten his grip on rival institutions.
Moscow, unlike western countries and some of Belarus's neighbours, has avoided any direct criticism of Lukashenko, who is the most pro-Russian of all leaders of post-Soviet states.

Despite his enthusiastic support for Moscow's goal of closer integration, the Belarussian leader's conflict with his opposition, his nostalgia for the Soviet Union and his hostility to economic reform have raised concern in Russia.

In the past week Lukashenko's prime minister has resigned and the president has sacked the head of the electoral commission, worsening his conflict with parliament whose leaders accuse him of trying to introduce a dictatorship.
